name: Skin Color Physiology Check
description: Validates skin color against physiological models including melanin/hemoglobin components — AI skin often lacks realistic color layering.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated or manipulated faces by analyzing whether skin color conforms to the biophysical constraints of real human skin:

1. **Skin Chromophore Decomposition**: Real human skin color is determined by the concentrations and distributions of a small number of chromophores — primarily melanin (in the epidermis) and hemoglobin (in the dermis). The method decomposes observed skin color into its constituent chromophore components using the Kubelka-Munk two-flux model of light transport in layered media. Given an observed skin reflectance spectrum R(λ), the model estimates: (a) melanin volume fraction (Cm, typically 1–43%), (b) oxygenated hemoglobin concentration (CHbO₂, typically 0.5–2.5 mg/mL), (c) deoxygenated hemoglobin concentration (CHb, typically 0.1–0.5 mg/mL), (d) epidermal thickness parameter. From RGB video, the method uses the three-channel constraint to estimate a reduced set of these parameters, exploiting the known absorption spectra of melanin (monotonically decreasing with wavelength) and hemoglobin (characteristic double absorption peak near 542 nm and 577 nm).

2. **Chromophore Spatial Distribution**: In real skin, chromophore concentrations vary spatially in physiologically constrained ways: (a) melanin varies with body region — the forehead is typically 10–20% darker than the inner arm, (b) hemoglobin concentration is higher in regions with higher blood vessel density — cheeks, nose tip, lips, and ears show higher redness, (c) the T-zone (forehead, nose, chin) has characteristic oiliness that affects specular reflection but not chromophore content, (d) the periorbital region shows distinctive bluish-purple tones from superficial venous blood. The method maps chromophore concentrations across facial regions and validates that the spatial distribution matches dermatological expectations. AI-generated faces often show uniform or incorrectly distributed skin color — missing the cheek blush, ear redness, or periorbital discoloration.

3. **Temporal Hemoglobin Dynamics**: In video, hemoglobin concentration varies with the cardiac cycle — each heartbeat sends a pulse of oxygenated blood to the face, causing subtle periodic color changes at 1–1.7 Hz (60–100 BPM). This photoplethysmographic (PPG) signal can be extracted from facial video using chrominance-based remote PPG (CHROM method). The method analyzes: (a) presence of a clear cardiac pulse in the 0.7–4 Hz band, (b) spatial coherence — the pulse signal should be detectable across all well-perfused facial regions with consistent phase, (c) pulse waveform shape — the systolic rise time (~100 ms) should be shorter than the diastolic descent, (d) signal-to-noise ratio > 2 dB. AI-generated faces typically lack any cardiac-cycle color variation, or show noise patterns inconsistent with physiological pulsation.

4. **Cross-Region Color Consistency**: The method validates that color relationships between different body parts follow physiological constraints: (a) both sides of the face should have approximately symmetric chromophore distributions (melanin asymmetry < 5%), (b) exposed and unexposed skin should show consistent melanin offset (tanning gradient), (c) lip color should show higher hemoglobin contribution than surrounding skin, (d) the sclera (whites of the eyes) should be spectrally distinct from skin. AI-generated faces may show color discontinuities at region boundaries, incorrect lip-to-skin color relationships, or eyes that blend chromatically with surrounding skin.
parameters:
Chromophore model: Kubelka-Munk two-flux
Melanin range: 1–43% volume fraction
Hemoglobin (HbO₂): 0.5–2.5 mg/mL
Hemoglobin (Hb): 0.1–0.5 mg/mL
rPPG method: CHROM (chrominance-based)
Cardiac frequency band: 0.7–4 Hz
Pulse SNR threshold: > 2 dB
Melanin asymmetry threshold: < 5%
Facial region segmentation: 68-point landmarks
Minimum face resolution: 128×128 pixels
accuracy: 80–90% accuracy detecting AI-generated faces via skin chromophore analysis. Temporal hemoglobin dynamics (rPPG) achieves AUC of 0.88. Spatial chromophore distribution provides F1-score of 0.85. Combined multi-channel analysis reaches 90% under controlled lighting. Performance decreases under extreme lighting conditions or heavy makeup.
source: Tsumura, N. et al. (2003). Image-based Skin Color and Texture Analysis/Synthesis by Extracting Hemoglobin and Melanin Information in the Skin. ACM TOG, 22(3), 770–779.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated faces through biophysical skin color violations. Remote physiological signal extraction for liveness detection. Forensic analysis of facial manipulation in video testimony. Complementing structural deepfake detection with physiological validation.
strengths:
• Based on biophysical skin optics — fundamental constraints on real skin color
• Temporal hemoglobin dynamics provide cardiac-cycle verification
• Spatial chromophore distribution is physiologically well-characterized
• Multiple independent channels (melanin, hemoglobin, rPPG) for robust detection
• Works across skin tones with appropriate model calibration
limitations:
• Requires visible skin (not occluded by masks, heavy makeup, or veils)
• Extreme lighting (colored lights, very dim) distorts chromophore estimation
• Video compression degrades subtle color variations needed for rPPG
• Some skin conditions (vitiligo, rosacea) alter expected distributions
• Advanced generators with explicit skin models may produce plausible color
